messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Graphic Designer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented, Compulsive Cleaning: I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control, Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Vignette:
Marta was 78, a European American woman who had spent most of her adult life in graphic design, a work she still described with a kind of practical pride. Even now, married and living with her husband in a quieter apartment than the one she had once shared in a storm-prone coastal town, she kept her desk arranged with a designer’s precision: pens lined up, papers squared, drawers labeled. That order mattered to her in the months after the flood that had upended her life. The disaster had come suddenly, in the middle of a night of ferocious rain and wind, when the river rose beyond its banks and water pushed into the neighborhood with terrifying speed. Marta remembered the sound first: doors banging somewhere in the building as people tried to hold them shut, then the heavy slam of her own apartment door jolting open and shut under pressure before she and her husband could brace it. In the chaos, she heard neighbors shouting about loved ones, and in the days that followed she was repeatedly exposed to conversations about people who had lost family members. Those words stayed with her in a raw, uncomfortable way, tied to the hours when she and her husband waited for the water to rise and for the electricity to fail.

In the weeks and months that followed, Marta found herself returning again and again to how it might have been prevented. She would sit at the kitchen table and dwell on the flood’s details, replaying weather reports, drainage systems, the timing of warnings, the decisions made by officials, and what should have been done differently. Her thoughts circled around the same points until they became exhausting, but she felt compelled to keep at them, as if some careful accounting might restore a sense of order. She also began cleaning and organizing repeatedly, sometimes wiping down already clean counters or rearranging pantry items and folders in straight lines. She said she did it to feel in control, especially when the world outside her door felt unpredictable. At other times she tried to erase the memory altogether, pushing it away when it surfaced, refusing to look at news coverage of storms or to revisit photographs from that period. Yet the memory did not stay in the past in the way she wished. Sometimes she could recall what happened, but felt completely numb, as if she were remembering something that had happened to a stranger. At other times the images were so immediate that the flood did not feel over at all; it came back with such force that she experienced it as happening right now. She found that this was especially true when a door opened abruptly or slammed somewhere nearby. In her current apartment, the sharp crack of the front door in the hallway or a cabinet door banging in the kitchen could pull her attention instantly back to the night the storm hit, leaving her tense and alert. She also noticed that talk about people losing loved ones had a particular sting, because it returned her to those bleak conversations after the disaster, when grief and helplessness seemed to fill every room. The smell of alcohol could also unsettle her, though she struggled to explain it except to say that it brought back the atmosphere of the aftermath, when people gathered in strained, numbed ways and she felt exposed to reminders she did not want.

Marta spoke about the flood with a kind of disbelief, saying that the memory felt so extreme it was hard to believe it actually happened to her. Even now she was convinced that the world was a dangerous place, and she said that her beliefs about how the world works had been completely destroyed. What had happened struck her as deeply unfair; nothing had been done to make it right, and that sense of injustice remained sharp. She did not describe herself as frightened in the abstract so much as constantly on guard, moving through daily life with the sense that ordinary things could turn threatening without warning. In her marriage, her husband had become accustomed to her checking doors and straightening things more than once, and though he tried to reassure her, she rarely found that reassurance lasting. At work, the practical demands of graphic design still appealed to her, but she found it harder to tolerate disruptions in her environment. A door slamming in the office corridor or the smell of alcohol from a coworker’s lunch could leave her distracted and unsettled for the rest of the day, making it difficult to settle back into the calm concentration her work usually required.

She sought help when she realized how much energy she was spending trying not to remember, not to think, not to feel taken by surprise again. At 78, she did not want the flood to keep intruding into her daily life with the same force, and she was tired of living as though every sudden sound might mean another disaster. What brought her to treatment was not only the persistence of the memories but the fear that the world had become permanently untrustworthy to her. She hoped that speaking about it might help her feel less trapped by the event, though what she feared most was that nothing could restore the sense of safety and fairness that the flood had taken from her.
